item.title: Pentagon Identifies Another Soldier Killed in Iran War
item.description:
The Pentagon on Tuesday released the name of a U.S. soldier killed during the disposal of an Iranian drone in northern Iraq.

Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30, of Fayetteville, N.C., died Saturday during a controlled detonation at Erbil Air Base. The incident is under investigation, the Pentagon said.

Sergeant Swinton had been assigned to the 108th Air Defense Artillery Brigade at Fort Bragg, in North Carolina.

Lt. Gen. John L. Rafferty, the commanding general of U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, said in a statement that Sergeant Swinton’s death had “occurred during an operation to safeguard fellow soldiers.”

“His service will not be forgotten,” General Rafferty added, “and his sacrifice is not in vain.”

Sergeant Swinton was not involved in the actual detonation, but was killed by flying debris from the blast, said a U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters.

The announcement came one day after the Pentagon released the names of two other soldiers killed in the war in recent days. They died in Jordan after an Iranian attack there on Friday. There have now been 17 American military personnel killed since the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.

The deaths occurred during a week of spiraling clashes between U.S. and Iranian forces in the Persian Gulf, where tensions have worsened since the collapse of a cease-fire reached by the countries last month.

As of Tuesday morning, U.S. forces had been striking targets in Iran, including military command centers and missile and drone launch sites, for 10 straight nights, according to U.S. Central Command. Iran said on Tuesday that it had attacked Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan, countries that host U.S. military bases.

The Iranian attack on Friday that killed two soldiers in Jordan also left another soldier missing, but remains found at the scene are believed to be those of the missing soldier.

In a text message to The New York Times, Sergeant Swinton’s mother, Christel Swinton Andujar, said her son was adventurous, fearless and “the kind of person who could light up any room.”

He grew up in Cumberland County, N.C., and loved basketball and fishing, his mother said. He was married and had two children.

“He had a contagious laugh, an incredible sense of humor and loved making people smile,” Ms. Swinton Andujar said. “He was a true jokester who believed life was meant to be lived to the fullest.”

He enlisted in the Army in 2017 as an air defense early warning system operator, according to the U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command.

The Army said in a statement on Tuesday that Sergeant Swinton would receive the Bronze Star, the Purple Heart and the Combat Action Badge, and that he would be posthumously promoted to staff sergeant.

“Sergeant Swinton was an experienced noncommissioned officer who took great pride in his work and the people around him,” said Brig. Gen. John Dawber, who leads the 32nd Army Air and Missile Defense Command. “He answered the call to duty with courage, honor and selfless dedication.”

“He was an amazing man,” Jamiah Gonzalez-Swinton, his wife, said tearfully when reached by phone on Tuesday morning. She was unable to say more.

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting. Kitty Bennett contributed research.

]]>

item.title: Trump Officials Withhold $1 Billion in Medicaid Funds From 2 States
item.description:
The Trump administration announced Tuesday it was withholding an additional $1 billion in Medicaid funds from California and Minnesota, the second time it has targeted the two states with Democratic governors for suspected fraud in their public health insurance programs.

The federal government will hold more than $867 million in payments from California and about $200 million from Minnesota until they can provide proof that certain claims were legitimate, officials said.

Federal officials said they had uncovered claims for care provided to Medicaid enrollees who were deceased, and had found health care providers billing for an unusually high number of patients, a possible sign of fraudulent activity. They said the problems in California and Minnesota were especially acute.

The administration has already been withholding around $250 million from Minnesota since February and $1.3 billion from California since May.

“If Gov. Gavin Newsom or Gov. Tim Walz wants this funding released, all they have to do is provide basic documentation showing that these services are legitimate and not fraudulent,” Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health and human services secretary, said at a news conference. “That’s common sense.”

Both governors criticized the Trump administration’s actions as politically motivated.

“California isn’t being targeted because Trump has evidence of fraud,” Governor Newsom posted on Twitter. “We are being targeted for political reasons.”

In a statement to The New York Times, Minnesota’s governor, Tim Walz, said that the Trump administration was only “punishing children, seniors, working families and people with disabilities.”

In April, a federal judge said that the administration’s actions were “historically unprecedented” but declined to intervene because it was a temporary pause on funding rather than a final decision.

The withheld funds make up a relatively small share of each of state’s Medicaid budget. California’s Medicaid program cost $150 billion in 2024, and Minnesota spent $18.6 billion.

In March, the White House announced a broad initiative to combat fraud across government programs nationwide, an effort being led by Vice President JD Vance. California and Minnesota have become frequent targets of the administration’s anti-fraud work.

In June, the Federal Bureau of Investigation published a list of “Most Wanted Fraudsters,” similar to the agency’s long-running list of most-wanted criminals, to help generate leads on individuals suspected of defrauding the government.

The Department of Justice announced Tuesday it had apprehended a person from that list: Khalid Satary, who was indicted in 2019, accused of billing Medicare over $500 million for expensive and unnecessary genetic tests.

Mr. Satary was apprehended in a Middle Eastern country and appeared in federal court Tuesday, a Justice Department spokesman said.

Minnesota’s Medicaid program experienced a recent, sharp rise in spending on behavioral therapy for children with autism, transportation services and a dozen other types of care it has since identified as “high risk.” Some of the services that providers billed the program for were never provided to patients, according to recent charges the Department of Justice brought against autism center owners and employees in May.

Dr. Mehmet Oz, the federal official who oversees Medicaid and Medicare, said Minnesota had recently cut off from its Medicaid program about 3,000 providers that had exhibited suspicious billing patterns. Most of the $200 million that the federal government has not released came from claims submitted by those providers before the state removed them, he said.

Minnesota has “disenrolled them for failed background checks, failed site visits and other issues,” Dr. Oz said. “This raises questions about the claims tied to these same providers in the quarter before they were removed.”

John Connolly, the temporary commissioner for the Minnesota Department of Human Services, said in a statement that the Trump administration had not provided the state with clear information on how certain funds were withheld.

He said he hoped the government would “share any information about their methods to identify potentially fraudulent providers in Minnesota.”

In California, Dr. Oz expressed concern about spending on “in-home support services,” where Medicaid pays for some enrollees to receive help with basic tasks including bathing, eating and taking medications.

He said that $391 million of the newly withheld funds had to do with questionable claims for that type of care, and that spending on in-home support had grown twice as quickly recently in California as it had in the rest of the nation.

In his Twitter post, Governor Newsom defended the additional spending on in-home care.

“Dr. Oz doesn’t understand that we are *SAVING* taxpayers money by keeping seniors and people with disabilities out of far more expensive nursing homes!” he wrote.

]]>

item.title: Senate Panel Advances Jay Clayton as Next Spy Chief on Party-Line Vote
item.description:
The Senate Intelligence Committee approved Jay Clayton on Tuesday as President Trump’s pick to oversee the U.S. intelligence community, clearing a key hurdle that may install Mr. Clayton in the job by the end of the week despite evaporating support from Democrats.

The vote, 9 to 8, fell along party lines, as every Republican on the panel backed Mr. Clayton while every Democrat voted in opposition.

Assuming he is confirmed by the full Senate as expected, Mr. Clayton will take command of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence from Bill Pulte, a housing official who has pursued campaigns of retribution against the president’s perceived enemies.

Mr. Clayton had been seen by some Democratic lawmakers as a palatable offering compared with Mr. Pulte, whom they excoriated as a Trump loyalist lacking national security experience. Weeks ago, Democrats and Republicans were working in tandem to quickly hold a hearing and secure a vote to confirm Mr. Clayton to the post in order to prevent Mr. Pulte from taking the job even briefly.

But Mr. Trump abruptly delayed the confirmation proceedings, ordering Mr. Clayton not to appear at the initial hearing, a move that allowed Mr. Pulte to take over from Tulsi Gabbard in the position of acting director.

During his short tenure atop the agency, Mr. Pulte oversaw staffing cuts and worked with others to declassify documents related to the 2020 election. But he has so far not fired as many people as Democrats had initially feared, and the documents the White House released last week concerning foreign election meddling were in many instances information that had already been made public.

Democratic senators were disappointed with Mr. Clayton’s performance in his confirmation hearing last week, finding his evasive answers about whether President Joseph R. Biden Jr. had won the 2020 election unsatisfying. Mr. Clayton, who serves as the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, said that Mr. Biden had been “certified” as the winner — a sort of standard answer for Trump administration nominees — but declined to more explicitly say that he was the rightful winner.

Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas, the Republican chairman of the Intelligence Committee, praised Mr. Clayton as a qualified nominee with “deep experience combating a wide range of national security threats.”

In Mr. Clayton’s U.S. attorney role, his office also issued subpoenas this month to several New York Times journalists who had recently published articles disclosing security concerns about Mr. Trump’s new Qatari-donated Air Force One jet.

At his hearing, Mr. Clayton offered few specifics about the matter, saying the subpoenas were part of “an ongoing national security investigation.” He said that the U.S. attorney’s office had consulted with the Justice Department in Washington, and that he had followed “procedures that we have in place to protect the First Amendment, and protect the freedom of the press, and not result in intimidation of journalists.”

Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat who sits on the panel, pointed to both the subpoenas and Mr. Clayton’s answers about the 2020 vote as reasons for his opposition. Citing legal motions by The Times, Mr. Wyden said there were “credible allegations that he provided false testimony to the committee during his hearing about intimidation subpoenas sent about New York Times reporting.”

A motion by lawyers for The Times unsealed on Monday disclosed that the Justice Department sought phone records from the reporters, as well as some of their family members. The motion noted that the highly aggressive moves called into question the accuracy of Mr. Clayton’s testimony, when he said his office had followed procedures meant to protect press freedom.

Instead, Mr. Wyden argued, the department appeared to have “repeatedly violated its own regulations in issuing its subpoenas” under Mr. Clayton’s watch.

item.title: Troy Jackson Tightens Hold on Democratic Senate Nomination in Maine
item.description:
Troy Jackson has further tightened his grip on Maine’s Democratic nomination for Senate.

Mr. Jackson, a logger and former state lawmaker, is set to appear on the ballot at Democrats’ nominating convention on Saturday in Bangor alongside just two other candidates who have won almost no public support from delegates: David Costello and Saundra Pelletier.

Hundreds of delegates aligned with Mr. Jackson were elected last weekend, giving him a seemingly insurmountable advantage that forced his leading primary rivals to suspend their campaigns.

The lack of well-known opponents appears to set up the convention as a celebration of Mr. Jackson’s nomination. His campaign announced on Monday that it was turning its effort toward defeating Senator Susan Collins, a five-term Republican, in a race widely seen as crucial to control of the Senate.

While the other top contenders had announced that they were withdrawing from the race, there had been indications that at least one of them hoped to appear on the ballot at the convention.

But when the state party announced on Tuesday which candidates had made the ballot, the other leading candidates were not included — meaning that they had not turned in the 500 verified signatures required for a spot.

They included Dr. Nirav Shah, a former public health official who came in second in the primary for governor in June; Shenna Bellows, the Maine secretary of state, who came in fourth in that race; and Jordan Wood, a progressive activist who placed third in the Democratic primary for Maine’s Second Congressional District. Dr. Shah had previously announced that he had gathered more than 800 signatures.

Dan Kleban, a brewery owner, qualified for the ballot but filed paperwork to withdraw, a representative of the Maine Democratic Party confirmed to The New York Times.

“I’m proud to throw my support behind @TroyJackson207 to beat Susan Collins and fight for working Mainers,” Mr. Kleban said in an X post on Tuesday announcing his withdrawal. He ran for the same Senate seat last fall, but dropped his bid.

Each candidate needed to collect 50 signatures per county in at least eight counties, a requirement that had some contenders bouncing among county meetings last weekend to find signatories. All of the signatures had to come from registered Democratic primary voters.

The wave of campaign suspensions prompted CNN to call off a debate on Thursday that was set to feature Mr. Jackson, Dr. Shah, Ms. Bellows and Mr. Wood.

While delegates still have until Saturday to change their minds, the likelihood that large numbers would abandon Mr. Jackson continues to diminish as the week goes on.

Mr. Costello, an environmental policy consultant, placed third in the Democratic primary for Senate in June. Ms. Pelletier, the chief executive of a pharmaceutical company focused on women’s health, is a first-time candidate.

The party remains on edge after Graham Platner, who won 72 percent of the vote in the Democratic primary for Senate in June, relinquished the nomination following an allegation of rape and a string of other scandals. The upheaval left Democrats rushing to find a new nominee to face Ms. Collins.

Just over 600 delegates will vote at the convention in Bangor on Saturday, including 500 who were elected over the weekend and 101 from the state Democratic Party committee. More than 17,000 Maine Democrats voted or otherwise participated in county meetings to elect delegates over the weekend, the party said, including nearly 3,700 delegate hopefuls. Voters overwhelmingly favored delegates who were committed to Mr. Jackson.

“Today’s certification marks another important milestone in this open, transparent, and inclusive nominating process,” Devon Murphy-Anderson, the executive director of the Maine Democratic Party, said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “We look forward to hearing directly from these candidates and bringing Democrats from every corner of Maine together on Saturday to choose the strongest nominee to defeat Susan Collins.”

Any candidate has the option to withdraw from the race before Saturday, according to the party.

item.title: Hegseth Estimates Iran War Has Cost $37.5 Billion
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, under questioning from lawmakers, said on Tuesday that the Defense Department’s latest estimate of the cost of the Iran war was $37.5 billion.

Mr. Hegseth gave the estimate during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing.

The figure is about a $12 billion increase over the $25 billion estimate he gave in late April, just before President Trump negotiated a temporary cease-fire with Iran.

Mr. Hegseth and the Trump administration are requesting as much as $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the Iran war and pay for new weapons and personnel.

The Pentagon is asking for $46 billion to expand production lines and accelerate delivery of high-demand munitions, like precision bombs, hypersonic missiles and counter-drone systems.

“This is a new request based on new realities of a world we face, stepping up to meet that moment,” Mr. Hegseth said.

Senate Democrats and some Republicans expressed doubts about the need for billions of war funding in addition to the $1.5 trillion the Pentagon was asking for in the upcoming defense budget.

“This administration has tried to sell this as an emergency request, but it may be better understood as an attempt to skirt the normal appropriations process,” said Senator Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee.

“The problem is not a lack of money, but poor planning,” she said. “So I’ll be blunt. The truth is, your request does not make a lot of sense.”

Mr. Hegseth blamed the Biden administration for the size of the Pentagon’s emergency funding request.

“This kind of spending is needed because of the gross negligence and neglect of the Biden administration inside our department,” Mr. Hegseth said. He spoke of the need to modernize the military as war was changing rapidly with the advent of cheap and plentiful drones.

Typically, the Pentagon modernization efforts are supposed to be paid for through the regular budget, rather than emergency supplemental requests of the sort Mr. Hegseth was asking for on Tuesday.

On July 8, President Trump declared that the cease-fire was over, and hostilities have resumed. Late last week an Iranian attack on a base in Jordan killed two U.S. soldiers and left another soldier missing, but remains found at the scene are believed to be those of the missing soldier.

At least 50 people in Iran have been killed in U.S. strikes since the truce ended, according to the Iranian authorities.
